chapter: Funerals, Mardi Gras and civil rights
title: Witnessing civil rights clashes and playing a fraternity at the University of Alabama
summary: He photographed beatings in Florida and played a fraternity party while the Alabama campus was blocked to a black student.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: So during that time, I mean, it seems like a transition period as far as like the Civil Rights Movement, were you involved in that directly or actively in any of that?

Well, while the Civil Rights Movement is going on, I can tell you some things that I witnessed some of the first riots, set-ins, and different other things that was going along with Dr. King and other people marching in different places, you know. So we had to, we were in different places when it happened, such as in Jacksonville, Florida. And I regret the day that I got, I took pictures of the first people being hit in the head and crammed into buses and denied a place to eat and all this kind of stuff. I took pictures from the balcony of a hotel where it was staying right down upon a big blue bus where they were just herding people into, in there like cattle and beating them on the heads because they were sitting at a counter to get something to eat. And the garbage men went on a strike and they left all the garbage all around because unlike in New Orleans there were mostly white men picked up garbage, black people picked up garbage in Florida and Alabama and so forth. So I witnessed all these things. Another thing I witnessed was we went to play a job with, his name was Google Eyes, his real name was Joe August. And he took a five piece band and we went to Alabama to play. At the same time, if I get the name wrong, I think it's Arthurine, somebody that was being denied an education to go to the University of Alabama. Alabama. And this was like on the north part of the campus where the state troopers and the governor and everybody were standing in front of the university so this black child could not come in to get an education. At the same time, on the south part of the campus, we were hired by a fraternity to play music. And we arrived there, time to play the job and so forth. And the state troopers just opened up, let us through. The kids came out and picked us up, each individually, picked us up and put us on their shoulders, stuffed whiskey in our pockets, money in our hands, and brought us in the fraternity houses. And we said, yeah, let's have a good time. You know?
So what did that say to you?
That said to me that they wanted us to entertain, but they didn't want us to be smart.
It was such a thing to see that we did.

You can't come here and get an education at the University of Alabama, but you can come here and entertain us, and we'll pay you. It was very confusing. It was very confusing coming, you know, because in the earlier days, we rode on the bus. We had to sit in the back of a screen. They would take the little piece of wood with the two iron bars, and if there were 17 seats in front of you, they'd move it back. And you had to get back on that last seat and so forth. All kind of things. The colored water here, the white water there. The colored entrance there. If you wanted to go to the Alphian Theater, you had to climb up five stories in the goddamn air and look over a balcony, you know, down to what looks to be now a little nine-inch television screen. That's how it looked to you. There were so many places. Black bands, I knew, they couldn't play at the major hotels. They couldn't play in the major places. We couldn't play in the auditorium. And there was so many things. And here it is, we in Alabama, they accepted us playing music and entertaining them, but they didn't want us to learn. It seems that that's the most inferior, inferior, or feared thing of the white community or the white man was to have an educated black. Because they were progressing real fast. And it's still happening. We still got the same problem today in a lot of cases. It's better? Oh, yeah, it's better. I can see it's better. But the young people of today don't appreciate the sacrifice that was made between that time. Because they think something's owed to them without them achieving it. It has to be given to them. Given, given. We, and I know my generation of people who are now 50s and 60s and so forth, we have to work at it. Right. Definitely. And we're still working at it. We're still working at letting them know that they have to work for it.
